% tagged-lists — a list whose markers the structure tree declares, both bulleted and
% numbered.
%
% One concern: does a declared label leave the item's text? lists.pdf is untagged, so
% it exercises the glyph rule in layout and says nothing about this path — and this path
% is the one every document in the corpus takes. The defect it was written for reached
% the output as "- ■ text" on 1363 items across six corpus files, 1242 of them in
% ISO 32000-2, because sectionize mapped neither Lbl nor LBody and folded the label's
% spans into the item's own text where the sink then wrote its own bullet in front.
%
% The numbered list is not a second copy of the same case. A bullet is losable: Markdown
% writes one itself, so an item that drops "•" reads correctly anyway and the defect is
% only a doubled glyph. A number is not — "1." is text the document says, Markdown has no
% syntax that restates it (a parser would renumber from its own count), and an item that
% drops it has lost a reference the prose points at. Those two failures need separate
% assertions, and only the tagged path can make the second one at all: a leading number
% is also what a heading and a table row open with, which is why ADR 0011 records ordered
% lists as unreachable from the glyph side. Here the producer declares it.
%
% Nesting is deliberately absent. lists.pdf covers depth, and mixing it in here would
% mean a single gold file asserting depth and marker together — so a regression in either
% one reads as the same failure.
%
% Build this one with lualatex, not pdflatex, for the reason clauses.tex records at
% length: pdfTeX's tagging backend writes /MCID 1 into every /MCR while the content
% stream draws an increasing sequence, so all but one structure element joins to nothing
% and the paragraphs fall out of the tree. The committed PDF means a clone never builds
% either.
\DocumentMetadata{pdfstandard=ua-2, tagging=on}
\documentclass{article}
\usepackage{lmodern}
\pagestyle{empty}
\begin{document}

\begin{itemize}
  \item First bulleted item.
  \item Second bulleted item.
  \item Third bulleted item.
\end{itemize}

\begin{enumerate}
  \item First numbered item.
  \item Second numbered item.
  \item Third numbered item.
\end{enumerate}

\end{document}
